answers.answer: chi is a composable Go HTTP routing library for services and REST APIs. Application authors register handlers and middleware; an application's net/http server invokes the router. The hello-world executable demonstrates main constructing chi and passing it to http.ListenAndServe. Tests also run routers through httptest servers.

Principal observed components: chi.go defines the public Router/Routes interfaces and constructor; mux.go implements request routing; tree.go holds radix-tree matching, method endpoints and route walking; context.go carries request routing state and URL parameters; chain.go composes middleware. The middleware package supplies optional wrappers, including logging and panic recovery. _examples contains runnable consumers. mux_test.go provides behavior tests and benchmarks. README documents usage. render and docgen are linked external companion repositories, not established here as local packages.

Go is the evidenced implementation language. The root Go module is github.com/go-chi/chi/v5 with go 1.24 and no require directives. Root files use package chi; middleware is a separate imported package; the hello-world example is package main. Integration uses standard net/http and context rather than a separate application framework. Tests use Go testing and net/http/httptest. Markdown supplies documentation. Exact CI/build automation is unknown: directory access failed and guessed workflow files were unavailable. No build or tests were executed.

Public use starts with chi.NewRouter(), which calls NewMux. Register routes with Get (and optionally Use middleware), then pass the router to http.ListenAndServe. The inbound HTTP boundary is (*Mux).ServeHTTP, satisfying Router's embedded http.Handler interface.

Dispatch is (*Mux).routeHTTP in mux.go: method/path selection → tree.FindRoute → handler.ServeHTTP, with 404/405 fallbacks. node.FindRoute delegates the actual radix traversal and endpoint-method matching to node.findRoute in tree.go.

Direct outbound dependencies, with call-site proof: RouteCtxKey/*Context assertion (418), methodMap lookup (436), mx.tree.FindRoute (442), Context.RoutePattern (448), MethodNotAllowedHandler (438/454), and NotFoundHandler (456). It reads URLParams and dynamically invokes the returned handler (450). Request.SetPathValue is a standard-library call (446). Context.RoutePattern joins and normalizes accumulated patterns.

TestMuxPlain registers the /hi callback that writes bye. Registration: NewRouter → NewMux; Get → handle → InsertRoute → setEndpoint stores the GET handler. Execution: testRequest constructs GET ts.URL+/hi; DefaultClient.Do crosses the HTTP transport/httptest-server boundary → Mux.ServeHTTP → computed handler → routeHTTP → FindRoute → findRoute → stored callback.ServeHTTP → ResponseWriter.Write. With no middleware, chain returns its endpoint directly. testRequest reads the response and the test compares it with bye. Server dispatch, interface/function calls and ResponseWriter are dynamic boundaries; this is a source trace, not an executed trial.
Two direct production Mux consumers: Find (354) and routeHTTP (442). Match is indirect through Find (340-341). Find performs introspection; routeHTTP executes the selected handler.

TestMuxPlain exercises the GET /hi dispatch and a missing-path fallback through httptest.NewServer plus testRequest. The helper performs an actual HTTP client request; the server's handler boundary reaches Mux.ServeHTTP and routing. TestMuxBasic additionally registers GET/HEAD/POST handlers and parameterized paths. These are identified tests, not claimed passing runs.

Input precedence: Context.RoutePath, URL.RawPath, URL.Path, then '/'; method override similarly precedes Request.Method. Tree traversal consumes static prefixes, captures delimiter-bounded parameters after regexp validation, and captures wildcard remainder; failed branches roll captures back. Registration extracts parameter names into endpoints; matching pairs those names with values. FindRoute resets local captures, appends successful captures into lifecycle URLParams, and records route patterns. URLParam reads this stack backwards; RoutePattern joins patterns and normalizes wildcards/slashes. Successful dispatch exports SetPathValue and Request.Pattern. Mount derives the next RoutePath from the wildcard and clears its public wildcard value. No URL-unescape step is evidenced in this routing path.
